name: Illinois
summary_text: Illinois stands under the national framework of the United States, where travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed federal agencies to use "sex" rather than "gender." The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are adjudicated only as M or F from supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed the restriction to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad. Entry screening carries separate exposure. An executive order issued 5 February 2025 on women's sports was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes would be barred from entering the country to compete in women's sports; visa applicants are flagged with an internal marking, and an applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth is treated as fraud carrying a permanent bar. Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller. Facilities rules at state level vary sharply. Bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools, and in some states to government buildings, cover 9 states and 1 territory, with trans use of facilities made a criminal offence in certain circumstances; 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. State-level identity documents are also being closed. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, which rights groups call a template for other state legislatures. Equality-map research shows that the conditions for changing a gender marker on a licence or birth certificate differ state by state. Custody is a documented site of harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement; severe sexual abuse was also widely reported. Official hostility extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups. A May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist. Care access is restricted on several fronts. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as mutilation and some hospitals paused care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, proposed health-department rules in October 2025 would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, and in July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on each measure should be checked before travel. Against that framework, Illinois sits at the protective end of state law. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills places Illinois in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier, whose laws are assessed as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights. The tier also includes California, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New York and Washington among its fourteen other members. Illinois holds a shield or refuge law, recorded as "State has shield law or executive order 2023" on the Movement Advancement Project Transgender Healthcare Equality Map with data as of 27 September 2026. The law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care that is legal in Illinois has been banned in the patient's home state, which bears directly on visitors travelling from ban states to receive care. The shield position is a minority one nationally. Sixteen states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold shields, while 32 states and 5 territories, covering 56%, hold none. A trans visitor to Illinois therefore reaches a jurisdiction with express statutory protection for care that a majority of states do not provide, while remaining subject to the federal document, entry and enforcement measures described above.

sources.title: HB 3930 - Illinois hate crime statute amendment
sources.documents: Addition of 'gender identity' to Illinois hate crime law, which since 1991 covered actual or perceived sexual orientation
sources.detail: Passed House April 16 and Senate May 20, 2015 unanimously; signed by Governor Bruce Rauner July 20, 2015; effective January 1, 2016

sources.title: Youth Mental Health Protection Act - conversion therapy ban
sources.documents: Prohibits mental health providers from practicing conversion therapy / sexual orientation change efforts on minors under 18; federal court limit for religious counseling
sources.detail: Passed House 68-43 May 19, 2015 and Senate 34-19 May 29; signed August 20, 2015; effective January 1, 2016; U.S. District Court for Northern District of Illinois dismissed pastors' suit Feb 15, 2017 as nonjusticiable - private religious counseling not 'trade or commerce'

sources.title: Illinois birth certificate and ID gender marker reforms
sources.documents: Removal of surgery requirement for legal gender change; process for M/F/X markers on birth certificates, driver's licenses and state IDs; recognition of transgender parent as birth parent
sources.detail: Reform bill passed 63-43 House, 32-22 Senate May 31, 2017, signed Aug 25, 2017 effective Jan 1, 2018; forms cited: 'Affidavit and Certificate of Correction Request', 'Declaration of Gender Transition/Intersex Condition', Secretary of State 'Gender Designation Change Form', $15 fee; X option July 2020 on birth certificates, from 2024 on licenses; 2023 re-introduced reform effective July 1; out-of-state-born change allowed since July 1, 2024; Lambda Legal-assisted transgender father case Jan 2020

name: Illinois
summary_text: Illinois stands under the national framework of the United States, where travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed federal agencies to use "sex" rather than "gender." The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are adjudicated only as M or F from supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed the restriction to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad. Entry screening carries separate exposure. An executive order issued 5 February 2025 on women's sports was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes would be barred from entering the country to compete in women's sports; visa applicants are flagged with an internal marking, and an applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth is treated as fraud carrying a permanent bar. Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller. Facilities rules at state level vary sharply. Bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools, and in some states to government buildings, cover 9 states and 1 territory, with trans use of facilities made a criminal offence in certain circumstances; 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. State-level identity documents are also being closed. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, which rights groups call a template for other state legislatures. Equality-map research shows that the conditions for changing a gender marker on a licence or birth certificate differ state by state. Custody is a documented site of harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement; severe sexual abuse was also widely reported. Official hostility extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups. A May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist. Care access is restricted on several fronts. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as mutilation and some hospitals paused care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, proposed health-department rules in October 2025 would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, and in July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on each measure should be checked before travel. Against that framework, Illinois sits at the protective end of state law. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills places Illinois in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier, whose laws are assessed as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights. The tier also includes California, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New York and Washington among its fourteen other members. Illinois holds a shield or refuge law, recorded as "State has shield law or executive order 2023" on the Movement Advancement Project Transgender Healthcare Equality Map with data as of 27 September 2026. The law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care that is legal in Illinois has been banned in the patient's home state, which bears directly on visitors travelling from ban states to receive care. The shield position is a minority one nationally. Sixteen states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold shields, while 32 states and 5 territories, covering 56%, hold none. A trans visitor to Illinois therefore reaches a jurisdiction with express statutory protection for care that a majority of states do not provide, while remaining subject to the federal document, entry and enforcement measures described above.
